---
title: "1. A MOS operating point is more than a current"
---

[Reading route](index.qmd) · [Next: common-source amplifier](02-common-source.qmd)

A useful transistor choice supplies the required current while leaving room
for the terminal voltages to move. Its current alone does not tell us how much
signal gain, output sensitivity or charging speed the circuit will obtain.
We need the operating point and the local response around it before choosing
width, length and how many physical units to place in parallel.

## Four terminals determine the conducting state

Consider the three equal NMOS units later used by R37:

```text
N0(D=out, G=gate, S=source, B=0) W=2.947220014 um L=0.40 um
N1(D=out, G=gate, S=source, B=0) W=2.947220014 um L=0.40 um
N2(D=out, G=gate, S=source, B=0) W=2.947220014 um L=0.40 um
```

The [full R37 circuit](../studies/gain-operating-point-accuracy/circuits/R37.cir)
connects a drain resistor to the supply and a source resistor to ground. For
an NMOS in its intended forward conducting state, increasing gate voltage
relative to source generally increases current entering the drain. The supply
provides the energy. The body also affects conduction; with `B=0`, a source
that rises above ground changes body bias as well as gate-to-source voltage.

Use differences, not absolute node labels:

$$V_{GS}=V_G-V_S,\qquad V_{DS}=V_D-V_S,\qquad V_{BS}=V_B-V_S.$$

For a PMOS near the positive rail, it is often easier to reason using positive
magnitudes $V_{SG}$ and $V_{SD}$: lowering the gate relative to its source
increases its source-to-drain conduction. We still report signed measured
currents according to the sensor direction. In these circuits, NMOS bodies
normally connect to ground and PMOS bodies to VDD. Reversing terminals, changing
body ties, or driving beyond the model's declared voltage domain is a different
case that needs its own support.

## Make a first prediction, then identify its limits

The elementary long-channel strong-inversion saturation approximation is

$$I_D\approx\tfrac12\mu C_{ox}(W/L)(V_{GS}-V_T)^2.$$

It suggests that increasing $W/L$ increases current at fixed overdrive and that
$g_m/I_D\approx2/(V_{GS}-V_T)$. This is a starting intuition under that model's
assumptions, not the sizing law used to generate the APM results. Short-channel
effects, moderate inversion, output conductance and body bias matter. A hard
threshold extracted from an operating-point printout is not a switch that
separates exactly zero current from square-law behavior.

For the saved R37 nominal point, the three-unit bank has $V_{GS}=0.447313$ V,
$I_D=32.497$ µA and $g_m=547.940$ µS. The printed device threshold is about
0.411211 V. Putting that threshold difference directly into the simple
$2/(V_{GS}-V_T)$ expression predicts about 55.4 V⁻¹; the saved model's actual
$g_m/I_D$ is **16.861 V⁻¹**. That large mismatch rejects the square-law shortcut
at this operating point. It does not invalidate the current/voltage observations.
Use the model's measured derivatives and supported terminal conditions for the
design, rather than forcing a familiar approximation to fit.

## Distinguish the slopes that control different errors

Around a fixed bias point, a first-order NMOS drain-current increment is

$$i_d=g_m v_{gs}+g_{ds}v_{ds}+g_{mb}v_{bs}.$$

$g_m$ is the derivative with respect to $V_{GS}$ while $V_{DS}$ and $V_{BS}$
are held fixed. $g_{ds}$ is the derivative with respect to $V_{DS}$ at fixed
control voltages; its inverse $r_o$ is the local output resistance. $g_{mb}$
describes the body-voltage contribution under the stated $V_{BS}$ convention.
All three have units A/V, or siemens. They sum across parallel units when
the units share the same terminal increments.

The ratio $g_m/I_D$ measures local current-control efficiency. The ratio
$g_m/g_{ds}$ estimates intrinsic voltage-gain potential with a high-impedance
load. Neither is the completed amplifier's gain: external load conductance,
source resistance and other transistors still enter the node equations.

| Saved nominal bank quantity | R37 | R75 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Physical NMOS units | 3 | 6 |
| Current, µA | 32.497 | 69.994 |
| gm, µS | 547.940 | 1231.172 |
| gds, µS | 1.573 | 3.486 |
| gmb, µS | 126.451 | 281.751 |
| gm/ID, V⁻¹ | 16.861 | 17.590 |
| Source voltage, mV | 2.685 | 12.027 |

These values come from the [saved OP/device records](../studies/learning-path-v1/data/resistor-op.json)
and the [recalculated bank quantities](../studies/learning-path-v1/summary.json).
They are summed derivatives of the actual units at their own circuit operating
points, not a new width sweep. R75's geometry and source resistor differ from
R37's; do not attribute every change in this table to current alone.

## Choose dimensions within a headroom and resource budget

Width, length and unit count affect different parts of the problem. At a given
current, a larger effective width can reduce required gate overdrive; it also
adds gate and junction charge. Length changes output conductance and the
current-density relation as well as physical area. In a calibrated variation
model, enlarging a device can change its uncertainty, but the relevant source
profile and the circuit's transmission path still matter. An area-only rule
cannot replace that calculation.

Our examples retain separate stable identities for each physical MOS unit.
This matters when a later Local realization assigns device-specific threshold
and mobility perturbations. One wide device and three independently varied
devices are not automatically the same complete sample, even if their nominal
total width matches. The examples use supported individual geometries rather
than treating multiplicity as an excuse to hide the unit inventory.

Headroom asks whether every device has enough terminal voltage for the intended
behavior throughout the required signal range. In R37, $V_{DS}$ is about
0.4973 V at nominal, while the printed saturation-voltage diagnostic is about
0.0877 V per unit. That leaves room at the center, but does not by itself prove
the required distortion or output swing. The output and source both move
during a signal, so recheck the actual terminal voltages along that trajectory.
A “saturation” label also does not mean $g_{ds}=0$.

This is a practical sizing sequence: specify the current and voltage task;
use equations to estimate the needed derivative; choose supported dimensions;
solve the complete finite circuit; then check which condition or cost limits
the intended use. The following chapters show actual redesign choices rather
than a universal optimum for $g_m/I_D$ or device length.

## A first look at diode connection

Tie a MOS drain to its gate and let a finite source supply current to that
node. The node voltage must settle where the MOS takes the supplied current:

```text
Diode NMOS: Nref(D=bias, G=bias, S=0, B=0)
```

With source and body fixed, a small rise in `bias` increases both $V_{GS}$ and
$V_{DS}$. The small-signal conductance looking into that combined node is
approximately $g_m+g_{ds}$, so its resistance is near $1/(g_m+g_{ds})$.
The node is neither a perfect voltage reference nor an ideal current source.
It will become the control voltage for a mirror in chapter 3, where we count
the finite source that sustains it.

You can now ask what the current buys: a local slope, output resistance, voltage
room and a resource cost. [Chapter 2](02-common-source.qmd) puts the same MOS
bank together with its load and solves the current balance that makes an
amplifier. For broader device characterization and gm/ID methodology, see
[Pretl, Koefinger and Dorrer, chapters 2–4](https://iic-jku.github.io/analog-circuit-design/aicd.html).
Their process examples are further reading; the APM numerical evidence above
comes from this site's own saved circuits.
